newsitem.title: UK: Gold slides to 40-month low, bumpy ride seen.
newsitem.headline: Gold slides to 40-month low, bumpy ride seen.

text.p: Gold prices slipped under $350.00 per ounce on Wednesday for the first time since mid September 1993, leaving market analysts predicting a bumpy ride ahead for the precious metal.
Later in the day, bullion fixed at $351.20 well down on Tuesday's $354.70 but reflecting a bounce from the low trade of $349.65 recorded in the morning.
"It's looking very weak," a London bullion dealer said, noting that some market players had forced the market lower in early trading by borrowing gold to sell on the spot market.

Part of that weakness reflected the soaring strength of the U.S. dollar against most of the other major currencies which made a dollar-priced commodity like gold unattractively expensive for buyers in marks or yens.
"It was a sentiment driven thing this a morning," said Rhona O'Connell, a market analyst at stockbroker T. Hoare and Co.

By the afternoon the market had picked up marginally. "New York looked nervous coming in, but prices managed a little bounce," a dealer said against a background of a steep fall on Wall Street and a dollar retreating from early gains.
"Part of the reason the Dow (Dow Jones Industrial average) was off was the IBM results were below expectations and that may have helped gold a little," O'Connell added.

Tuesday's upbeat remarks on the U.S. economy and inflation by U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan sent the dollar to a 46-month highs of 118.75 yen and further stretched its value against the mark.
The net result was to turn investors away from gold.
European stock markets also shot to record highs on Wednesday on the back of Greenspan's speech and Wall Street's strong performance on Tuesday.
Gold has been unable to compete with the soaring stocks and bond markets in Europe and the U.S. for investors' attention.
Ironically in Japan where stock prices have been falling, investors have been forced to sell gold futures to meet calls against their crumbling paper assets.
Many market professionals saw gold slipping lower before the market began to look healthier.
"We haven't even had a 10-dollar day never mind a 20-dollar day," one dealer said adding that a really swingeing fall in price might clear the market's system and let it start building afresh.

But O'Connell for one was less convinced another deep fall was likely. "I can see $348 or maybe a little lower but the incentive to short the market (sell gold yet to be boughtin the expectation of a price fall allowing it to be bought later at a cheaper price) will get less as profit margins are squeezed by a slower price decline," she said.
"Some people think that could come sooner rather than later," she added.
But behind the market's rather diffident hopes was the alarming prospect of other European central banks following the example set by the Netherlands and selling gold from their reserves.
The Dutch sale of 300 tonnes announced last week plunged an already gloomy gold market into a state of near morbidity.
Prices had fallen by 3.5 percent since the beginning of the year on rumours of an institutional sale and after a sigh of relief that the truth was out, they resumed their decent.
"The fear of a copy-cat sale has overwhelmed any feeling of relief," said bullion market analyst Andy Smith at Union Bank of Switzerland.
Smith said one possible safety net for gold was in the more thinly traded "white" metals -- silver, platinum and palladium -- which had been losing value largely in line with gold.

"There is less structural change in the market for the white metals than in gold and so the smart money might sniff around them as a way of investing in the sector wich could support gold," he suggested.
"There is no question we are on a cusp here. But my feeling is there is so much bearishness around that the price might whipsaw up rather than go into another fall," he added.
T. Hoare's O'Connell saw another possible saviour for gold. The usually secretive London Bullion Market Association is shortly to begin releasing details of turnover figures from the market.
"That could come at a good time," she said. "It will show investors the depth of the market and could be re-assuring at a time when the price is falling."
Gold's highest fix was on January 21, 1980, when it hit $850 per ounce when the threat of higher oil prices and galloping inflation sent investors scurrying to gold as a safe haven.
But ever since prices have been in overall decline.
Gold reached its highest level since 1990 in a brief rally last year which took it to $416.25 on February 2, its highest price for six years.
